faq.a: WYSIWYG stands for “What You See Is What You Get.” In computing it describes editors that show the final result as you work; about a person, it means they are exactly as they appear.

faq.q: Where did the phrase “what you see is what you get” come from?
faq.a: The phrase was in popular use before computers, and comedian Flip Wilson helped make it famous in the early 1970s through his character Geraldine. The acronym later spread with visual computer editors.
A WYSIWYG leader is consistent and transparent, with words that match actions and the same character in every setting. People don’t have to guess what they really think.

faq.q: Is being WYSIWYG the same as being blunt?
faq.a: No. Genuine transparency includes care and good judgment. It means being honest and consistent, not saying everything you think as harshly as possible.

faq.q: How can I become a more consistent leader?
faq.a: Clarify your values, keep the promises you make, treat people the same regardless of their status, and ask trusted colleagues where you seem inconsistent.
